chapters.title: About This Book
paragraphs: Frankenstein was written by Mary Shelley when she was eighteen years old, and it changed literature forever. In the summer of 1816, the so-called Year Without a Summer, she was staying by Lake Geneva with the poets Lord Byron and Percy Shelley. To pass the stormy evenings, Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Mary struggled for days until a nightmare gave her the image: a pale student kneeling beside the thing he had put together, watching the dull yellow eye of the creature open. She woke up and began to write.

The novel was published anonymously in 1818 with the subtitle The Modern Prometheus. It tells of Victor Frankenstein, a brilliant young scientist who discovers the secret of giving life to dead matter, creates a living being, and then abandons it in horror. The creature, intelligent and sensitive, learns to speak and read, begs for compassion, and, when refused, turns to vengeance. It is at once a Gothic horror story, a tragedy, and a profound moral fable about responsibility.

Frankenstein is often called the first science fiction novel, because its horror comes not from ghosts or demons but from science itself, from a man who reaches beyond the limits of what human beings should attempt. Two hundred years later, every story about artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, or inventions that escape their inventors is still living in the shadow of this book. The real monster of the story may not be the creature at all, but the creator who refused to take responsibility for what he made.

chapters.title: Letters from the Arctic
paragraphs: The story begins not with Victor Frankenstein but with another ambitious young man, in another frozen wilderness. Robert Walton, an English sea captain, writes home to his sister from the far north, where he is leading an expedition toward the North Pole. His first letter opens with the formal courtesy of the age: "To Mrs. Saville, England. St. Petersburgh, Dec. 11th, 17—."

Walton is burning with a dream. He wants to be the first man to reach the Pole, to discover the secret of the compass, to open new lands to science. But he confesses to his sister that he has one great sorrow: he has no friend. He is surrounded by rough sailors, brave men but uneducated, and he longs for a companion with a mind like his own, someone with whom he can share his hopes and fears. It is a lonely, romantic ambition, and it will lead him into terrible danger.

He had spent six years preparing for this voyage, reading every account of Arctic exploration, hardening his body against cold and hunger and sleeplessness. He was, in his way, as much a dreamer as Victor himself, and Victor would see it at once. When the stranger first opened his eyes aboard the ship, his earliest questions were about the course they sailed. Learning that they headed north, toward the Pole, he wept with a strange and terrible joy, for his enemy had fled north too, and the chase could go on.

The sailors had never seen anything like it. Through the telescope, the distant figure on the sledge seemed of gigantic stature, far beyond any man, driving its dogs across the ice with a speed no human team could match. It vanished into the mist, and the men crossed themselves and whispered of spirits. Walton, a man of science, laughed at their superstitions, but he recorded the sighting carefully in his journal. He did not know that he had just seen the creature, fleeing north with Victor Frankenstein only a day behind it.

As his ship pushes through the ice, the sailors see something impossible: far off on the ice, a gigantic figure on a sledge, drawn by dogs, moving with inhuman speed. Hours later they find another sledge, broken and half-buried, and on it a dying European, thin as a skeleton, half-frozen, raving about someone he is pursuing. They bring him aboard, and slowly, as warmth returns to his body, the stranger begins to speak. His name is Victor Frankenstein, and he has been chasing a demon across the ice. When Walton begs to hear his story, Victor agrees, but with a warning: listen, he says, and learn from my destruction. What follows is one of the strangest confessions ever written.

Victor tells of his childhood in Geneva, a happy boy with a loving family, and of his hunger for knowledge. At the university of Ingolstadt he threw himself into the new science of electricity and chemistry. His professors, Waldman and Krempe, opened his eyes to the wonders of modern discovery. And then, in his laboratory, working alone through nights of feverish labour, he stumbled upon the secret he had been seeking: the principle by which life itself could be given to lifeless matter. He does not explain the secret in his story. He only says that he learned how to bestow animation upon lifeless matter, and that from that moment he was possessed by a single thought: to create a living being, a new species that would bless him as its creator.

Walton listened spellbound, and saw in Victor the very friend he had been longing for: a man of genius, of deep feeling, of grand ambition brought low by suffering. He wrote to his sister that he had found the companion of his dreams, and that he would set down Victor's story exactly as he heard it, as both a warning and a memorial. The tale that follows, then, reaches us through two voices: Victor's confession, written down by Walton in his letters home, carried across the ice and the sea to England.

chapters.title: The Dreary Night of November
paragraphs: For months Victor laboured in his workshop, collecting bones and organs, assembling a frame larger than any human being, eight feet tall, with limbs in proportion. He chose beautiful features for his creature, lustrous black hair, white teeth, a noble brow, dreaming of the gratitude this new Adam would feel toward him. He worked in secret, cut off from his family, his health breaking, his mind fixed on a single goal. And then, on the night when his work was complete, the moment came.

"It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils." The rain pattered against the windowpanes, the candle was nearly burnt out, and by its dim light Victor saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open. It breathed hard. A convulsive motion agitated its limbs. The thing he had made was alive.

Victor had imagined this moment a thousand times, and in every imagining it was glorious. He would breathe life into dead matter, and a new race would rise up and call him father. But the reality was otherwise. As the creature's limbs began to move, as the unnatural life flickered behind those yellow eyes, Victor felt not triumph but a cold horror spreading through his chest. He had not created a man. He had created a mockery of one, and in that instant he understood, too late, that knowledge without wisdom is a curse.

What followed was not triumph but horror. The beauty of Victor's dream vanished in an instant. The yellow skin barely covered the muscles beneath, the eyes were watery and staring, the whole creature was a wretched, loathsome thing. Victor had dreamed of a blessing and woken to a nightmare. He rushed from the room, then from the house, and spent the night walking the empty streets of Ingolstadt in an agony of fear and guilt. When morning came and he dared to return, the creature was gone.

Victor fell into a fever that nearly killed him, nursed back to life by his dear friend Henry Clerval, who had come to visit. For months Victor said nothing of what he had done. He tried to forget. But forgetting was impossible, because the creature he had abandoned was learning to live, and it would not stay silent forever. Victor had given life, and then, in the moment that mattered most, he had refused the responsibility of a creator. That refusal is the true crime of the novel, and everything that follows flows from it like poison from a wound.

In the days before that night, Victor had been the brightest student at Ingolstadt. Professor Waldman had praised his extraordinary talent, and his fellow students marvelled at his tireless energy. He had studied the decay of bodies and the spark of electricity, the ancient dreams of the alchemists and the modern triumphs of chemistry, until all his knowledge fused into a single terrible insight. He told Walton afterward that he would give anything to unlearn the secret, that some doors, once opened, can never be closed again.

When Victor fled the workshop that morning, he ran through the empty streets as the church bells rang, laughing and weeping by turns, until he collapsed senseless. Clerval found him there and carried him home, and for months Victor lay in a nervous fever, haunted in his dreams by the creature's dull yellow eye. Even when his body recovered, his mind did not. Every shadow seemed to move, every knock at the door stopped his heart. He wrote to his family in Geneva with forced cheerfulness, but between the lines his letters trembled with a fear he dared not name.

chapters.title: The Creature Alone
paragraphs: While Victor lay in his fever, the creature wandered into the world alone, with no name, no language, and no friend. Its first sensations were a confusion of light and darkness, hunger and cold. It learned to find berries in the woods, to drink from streams, to hide from the human beings who screamed and threw stones at the sight of its face. It was not born evil. It was born innocent, and the world taught it fear before it ever learned a word.

At last the creature found shelter in a hovel attached to a cottage, where it could watch a family through a crack in the wall without being seen. The family were the De Laceys: a blind old father and his gentle children, Felix and Agatha, exiles living in poverty. Through the long winter the creature watched them, and from them it learned what it meant to be human. It learned language by listening to their lessons, for they were teaching a young Arabian girl named Safie to speak, and the creature learned alongside her, word by word.

It was the most moving education in all of literature, and the most tragic. The creature learned to admire the virtues of the De Laceys, their kindness, their music, their love for one another, and it began to dream that it too might be loved. It found books in the woods: Milton's Paradise Lost, Plutarch's Lives, and Goethe's Sorrows of Werter. From them it learned about good and evil, about heroes and monsters, about love and despair. It began to think of itself as Adam, the first of a new kind, and then, bitterly, as Satan, cast out and alone.

One day, gathering its courage, the creature revealed itself to the blind old father, who could not see its deformity and listened to its story with kindness. For a shining moment it seemed the creature might be accepted. But then Felix returned, saw the monster kneeling before his father, and drove it away with blows. The family fled the cottage that very night. The creature, rejected once more, burned the cottage to the ground and set out to find its creator. It had learned one terrible lesson from human beings: that it would never be loved for what it was. From that day, its heart began to turn toward revenge.

The cottagers never knew how closely they were watched. The creature learned to chop wood silently in the night and leave it stacked at their door, an invisible benefactor. It wept when Agatha played her guitar, and its heart swelled when Felix read aloud to Safie from the history of nations. Through Safie's lessons it learned the names of things: bread and fire, moon and star, father and friend. Each new word was a treasure, and each treasure made its loneliness sharper, for it had words now for everything in the world except what it was itself.

The books it found in the woods changed it forever. In Paradise Lost it read of Adam, created perfect and loved by his maker, and of Satan, cast out for his rebellion, and it could not decide which of the two it resembled more. In Plutarch's Lives it learned of great men and noble deeds. In the Sorrows of Werter it learned of love and of suicide. Knowledge, which Victor had pursued as a blessing, became for the creature a curse, for it taught the creature exactly what it could never have.

On the way to Geneva, the creature met Victor's little brother William in the woods and, learning the boy's name was Frankenstein, murdered him in a fury, framing the innocent servant Justine for the crime. Justine was hanged for a murder she did not commit. Victor knew the truth but said nothing, paralyzed by guilt and fear. The creature had struck its first blow, and it was only the beginning.

Justine's trial was the darkest hour of Victor's life before the greater darkness came. The poor girl, innocent and beloved by the whole household, was condemned on false evidence: William's locket, which the creature had planted in her pocket as she slept. She went to the scaffold confessing to a murder she had not committed, hoping for mercy in heaven if she could find none on earth. Victor, who could have saved her with a single word of truth, stood silent in the courtroom, and her death stained his soul forever.

chapters.title: You Are My Creator, But I Am Your Master
paragraphs: Victor fled to the mountains, to the glaciers above Chamonix, hoping the cold and the silence would calm his tormented mind. But on the ice, moving with impossible speed, came a figure he knew too well. The creature confronted him, and Victor, in horror and rage, cursed it and ordered it away. The creature did not move. It spoke, and its words were the most eloquent in the novel.

"You are my creator, but I am your master; obey!" The creature demanded to be heard. It told Victor its whole history: its loneliness, its education, its rejection, its crimes. It argued with terrible logic that it had been born good, that misery had made it a fiend, and that Victor, who had given it life and then abandoned it, owed it happiness. "I am malicious because I am miserable," it said. "Am I not shunned and hated by all mankind?"

Victor cursed the creature and called it demon, devil, wretch, but the creature answered him calmly, and its calm was more terrible than any rage. It reminded him that it had never asked to be born, that it had come into the world innocent, and that every crime it had committed had been taught to it by the cruelty of others. It spoke of the De Laceys with tenderness, of little William with remorse, of Justine with a grief that surprised even Victor. For a moment, listening on the ice with the mountains watching, Victor felt the stirrings of something like pity. Then he remembered Elizabeth, and his heart hardened again.

Then the creature made its demand, the demand on which everything would turn. "You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being." Give me a companion, it said, a creature as deformed as myself, and we will leave human beings forever. We will live in the wilds of South America, harming no one, content with each other. Refuse, and I will destroy everything you love, until you are as alone as I am.

Victor was torn apart. At first he refused, then, fearing for his family, he agreed. He travelled to Scotland, to a lonely island in the Orkneys, and there, in a hut above the sea, he began the dreadful work a second time. But as the months passed and the half-finished female lay on his table, his conscience rebelled. What if the two creatures bred a race of monsters? What if he unleashed a plague upon the earth? One night, with the creature watching through the window, Victor tore his work apart and destroyed it.

The creature's howl of despair echoed across the island. It had watched its last hope die. "You have destroyed the work which you began," it said. "I shall be with you on your wedding night." Victor did not understand the threat, or would not. He returned to Geneva and married his beloved Elizabeth, and on their wedding night, while Victor searched the house with a pistol, the creature slipped into the bridal chamber and strangled Elizabeth in her bed. Victor's father died of grief. Henry Clerval, his dearest friend, had already been murdered by the creature on the Irish coast. Everyone Victor loved was gone, destroyed by the being he had made and abandoned. There was nothing left for him now but revenge.

The wedding had been planned for joy, and Elizabeth, beautiful and kind, suspected nothing of the shadow hanging over her husband. On the wedding night Victor armed himself and searched every corridor of the house, convinced the creature meant to murder him. It was his last and greatest mistake. While he guarded the stairs with a pistol in his hand, the creature slipped through the window of the bridal chamber, and Elizabeth's scream told Victor, too late, what the threat had truly meant. He found her lifeless upon the bed, and his reason nearly left him forever.

Victor's old father, who had already buried his wife and his youngest son, could not survive this final blow. He died within days, and Victor stood utterly alone in the world, with no family left to protect and no reason left to live except one: to hunt the creature down and destroy it, or die in the attempt. He bought pistols and daggers, learned to live on almost no food and less sleep, and set out after his enemy with the single-minded fury of a man who has nothing more to lose.

chapters.title: The Chase on the Ice
paragraphs: Victor Frankenstein became a hunter. He followed the creature across Europe and into the frozen north of Russia, living on rage alone, sleeping in the snow, eating when he could. The creature always stayed a little ahead, leaving messages scratched in the ice, taunting its creator, drawing him onward toward the Pole. It was a pursuit with no end except death, two miserable beings locked together, each the other's torment and purpose.

At last Victor's strength failed. Walton's sailors found him on the ice, half-dead, still raving about his enemy. Aboard the ship, in the cabin, Victor told Walton his whole story as a warning, begging him to abandon his own reckless ambition before it destroyed him too. Then, worn out by suffering, Victor Frankenstein died. Walton closed his eyes and wept for a man he had known only a few weeks but had come to love like a brother.

In the dead of night, Walton heard a sound in the cabin. He entered and found the creature there, weeping over the body of its creator. It was a moment of terrible pity. The creature spoke to Walton, and its words were its own confession and its own condemnation. It had intended to make Victor as wretched as itself, and it had succeeded, but victory had brought no joy. "I shall die," it said, "and what I now feel be no longer felt." It had planned to burn itself on a funeral pyre in the far north, so that no trace of its miserable existence would remain.

Walton himself had faced a mutiny of the heart during those weeks. His crew, trapped in the ice and terrified by the endless white desert, begged him to turn back, and for a time he wavered. Victor, dying, urged him with his last strength not to abandon his glorious ambition, to be resolute and finish what he had begun. But Walton looked at his suffering sailors, thought of his sister waiting in England, and chose mercy over glory. He promised the dying man that he would turn the ship homeward when the ice released them. It was the one lesson of the whole tragedy that someone finally learned: that ambition must answer to love.

Walton tried to speak, but the creature would not be comforted. It had lost everything: its creator, its enemy, its accuser, its only companion in misery. With a final cry of despair, it sprang from the cabin window onto an ice raft that lay beside the ship. Walton watched from the deck as the raft was carried away on the dark waves. "He was soon borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance." The ice closed behind it. The story was over, and the Arctic silence fell again, as if none of it had ever happened.

chapters.title: The Hovel by the Cottage
paragraphs: Driven from village to village with stones and curses, the creature fled deeper into the forest until it reached a wilder, lonelier country. There, half-hidden among the trees, stood a small cottage, and attached to one side of it a low hovel, a miserable shed of boards and straw that had once sheltered animals. The hovel was dark and narrow, but it had one precious feature: through a chink in the wooden wall, the creature could see into the lighted room of the cottage beyond without being seen itself. It made this hovel its home, lining the damp floor with straw, and from that secret hiding place it began the strangest education any living being ever received.

The cottage was home to three people. There was an old man, blind, with silver hair, who spent his hours playing a gentle guitar and listening to the voices around him. There was a young man, handsome and sorrowful, who worked in the woods from dawn until dusk. And there was a young woman, gentle and fair, who kept the little house and sang softly as she worked. Their names, the creature soon learned, were De Lacey the father, and Felix and Agatha his children. They spoke French, a language the creature did not yet know, but it watched their faces and their gestures until it began to understand that these people, though poor, loved one another deeply.

The creature soon learned how this gentle family had come to such poverty. They had once been wealthy and honoured in Paris, but Felix had destroyed their fortune by an act of generosity. A Turkish merchant, unjustly accused and condemned to death, had been saved by Felix, who helped him escape from prison. For this crime of compassion Felix himself was imprisoned, his property seized, his name disgraced. Though the merchant went free, the De Laceys never recovered what they had lost, and they fled to Germany to live in obscure exile. The creature listened to this history with a burning heart, for it saw in Felix a mirror of its own fate: punished by the world for the crime of kindness.

They were exiles, and poverty was their constant companion. The creature watched Felix labour all day and return with only a scanty meal, watched Agatha divide the bread so that her father and brother had the larger share, watched the old man try to hide his grief behind his music. The sight filled the creature with a pity it had never felt before. It discovered that it could help them without revealing itself: in the dead of night it took Felix's tools and chopped firewood, stacking it silently at the cottage door. In the morning the family marvelled at the mysterious gift, and the creature, hidden in its hovel, felt the first warm pleasure of its life.

Then one day a stranger arrived who changed everything. A young woman rode up to the cottage on horseback, dark-eyed and beautiful, dressed in foreign clothes, and the whole family rushed out to embrace her with cries of joy. Her name was Safie. She was Arabian, and she spoke almost no French. Because she could not understand them, Felix began to teach her the language, slowly and patiently, naming the objects around them and repeating the words until she could say them back. The creature, listening through its chink in the wall, became her silent fellow pupil. Word by word, lesson by lesson, it learned French alongside Safie, until the confused sounds of human speech resolved into meaning.

Alone in the hovel, the creature began to practise the miracle of speech. It shaped its mouth around the sounds it heard through the wall, repeating them in a hoarse whisper until the syllables came clear: Felix, Agatha, bread, fire, moon. The first time it understood a whole sentence of the cottagers' talk, it trembled with a joy so fierce it frightened itself. Language was a key, and every new word unlocked another room of the human world. It spoke to the trees and the stream, holding long one-sided conversations, preparing for the day when it would have someone to answer.

In the evenings the cottage had its rituals, and the creature came to love them as a starving man loves bread. The old man would take up his guitar and play the soft airs of his lost France, and Agatha would sing in a voice so sweet that the creature wept without knowing why. Sometimes Felix read aloud while the others listened, and the firelight flickered on their peaceful faces. The creature, crouching in the cold dark of its hovel, pressed its eye to the chink and drank in every note, every word, every smile, hoarding them like a miser hoards gold.

From the lessons and the family's talk, the creature pieced together Safie's story. She was the daughter of a Turkish merchant living in Paris, and Felix had once saved that merchant's life when he was unjustly condemned by the French government. In gratitude the merchant promised Felix his daughter's hand, but when the time came he betrayed the promise and carried Safie away, meaning to keep both his daughter and his fortune. Felix was ruined and exiled for his part in the affair, and his father went blind with grief. Safie, who loved Felix and despised her father's treachery, escaped with her jewels, crossed Europe alone, and found her way to the cottage in Germany. It was a tale of injustice and courage, and the creature wept for it in the darkness of its hovel.

In those same woods the creature made another discovery that completed its education. It found a leather portmanteau, lost by some traveller, containing three books: Paradise Lost, a volume of Plutarch's Lives, and The Sorrows of Young Werter. By the light of the moon it taught itself to read more deeply, sounding out the words it had learned from Safie's lessons. The first of the books opened with lines that struck the creature like a blow, the words of Adam crying out to his Creator: "Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man? Did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?" The creature read them again and again, for it felt that Adam was speaking for it too.

But the books and the lessons also awakened questions that no one in the cottage could answer. Who was it, this being that could learn and feel and weep? Where had it come from, and why had it been made so different from all other living things? It remembered nothing before the workshop, the confused agony of its first days, the flight through the forest. Somewhere there was a maker, a father of its miserable existence, who owed it answers. The creature resolved that one day it would find this creator and demand to know why it had been brought into a world that had no place for it.

Each book taught the creature something different, and each lesson cut deeper. From Paradise Lost it learned of Adam, created perfect and beloved by his maker, and of Satan, proud and rebellious, cast out into misery; it studied both portraits and saw itself by turns in each of them. From Plutarch's Lives it learned of the great men of Greece and Rome, of courage, justice, and self-sacrifice, and it burned with admiration for virtues it could never practise. From the Sorrows of Werter it learned of tender love and of despair, of a sensitive soul destroyed by a world that had no place for it. Knowledge, which Victor had chased as the highest blessing, became for the creature the keenest curse, because every book showed it exactly what it was missing.

As the months passed, the creature watched the love between Felix and Safie deepen, and the sight was both beautiful and tormenting. It saw them walk together in the garden, saw Felix teach her the names of the flowers, saw the tenderness in their glances. No one would ever look at the creature so. Yet instead of bitterness, the sight filled it with a fierce resolve: it would become worthy of such love by becoming good. It would learn everything the De Laceys could teach, and one day it would lay its gentle heart at their feet.

Through Felix's readings to Safie the creature also learned the history of mankind, for in the evenings Felix read aloud from Volney's Ruins of Empires, a history of fallen kingdoms and ancient wars. The creature listened, spellbound, as the book told of empires rising in virtue and collapsing in corruption, of the grandeur and the wickedness of which human beings were capable. It filled the creature with a painful wonder: could the same species that produced the gentle De Laceys also produce the tyrants and murderers of history? The question troubled its sleep, for it sensed, without yet understanding, that it was about to learn the darker answer for itself.

As the winter deepened, the cottagers became the whole of the creature's existence. It lived for the sound of their voices through the wall and shaped its days around their comings and goings. In long solitary hours it imagined stepping from its hiding place to be received among them: Agatha smiling, the old man taking its hand, Felix clasping it as a brother. Some wiser part of it knew these dreams were folly, but they were the only warmth in its frozen life, and it clung to them. It was this dream, more than any book or lesson, that at last gave it the courage to knock on the cottage door.

And yet, even then, hope was not dead. The creature watched the blind old man and thought: he cannot see my face, so he cannot judge me by it. If I reveal myself to him alone, in the absence of the others, perhaps his kindness will make a place for me. It began to prepare, rehearsing the words it would say, dreaming of the day when it would knock at the cottage door and be welcomed in. It was the most innocent plan the creature ever formed, and it would end in the cruellest disappointment of its life.

chapters.title: The Blind Old Man
paragraphs: The creature chose its moment with care. One morning Felix, Agatha, and Safie all left the cottage together, and only the blind old De Lacey remained, sitting alone in the sun with his guitar silent on his knee. The creature had rehearsed its speech a hundred times in the hovel. It would present itself as a traveller, a friendless wanderer seeking kindness. It would win the old man's heart first, and through him, the hearts of the children. Trembling with a hope it had never dared to feel before, it lifted the latch and stepped into the cottage.

For days the creature prepared itself for the meeting. It practised its words aloud in the hovel until they flowed smoothly, choosing the simplest phrases it knew so that nothing would betray the strangeness of its voice. It washed its face in the stream and tried to arrange its coarse hair, as if neatness could soften what nature had made terrible. Again and again it imagined the old man's kindly face turning toward it, imagined the words of welcome, imagined Felix and Agatha returning to find a new friend seated beside their father. The fantasy was so vivid that the creature sometimes forgot, for an hour together, what it was.

The old man heard the step and turned his sightless face toward it. The creature spoke, and its voice, rough from disuse but gentle with longing, told a careful tale: it was a stranger, alone in the world, rejected by all who saw it, seeking only a little human kindness. Old De Lacey listened with a compassion that shone from his blind face. He spoke of the beauty of doing good, of the duty to comfort the afflicted, and he promised the creature that his children, though they might be startled at first, would learn to love a friend of their father. For a few shining minutes, the creature believed that its long loneliness was over.

The old man went on speaking, and his words fell on the creature's heart like rain on parched earth. He said that to comfort the afflicted was among the noblest duties of mankind, and that no misfortune should shut a sufferer out from human sympathy. The creature wept as it listened, great silent tears rolling down its hideous face, and when it tried to thank him its voice broke with feeling. In that moment it loved the blind old man as it had never loved any living thing, for he was the first human being who had ever spoken to it with kindness.

Then the door opened, and everything was destroyed in an instant. Felix returned first, and stopped dead at the sight of the gigantic figure kneeling before his blind father. With a cry of horror he seized a stick and struck the creature with all his strength, driving it to the ground. Agatha screamed and fainted. Safie fled from the room in terror. The creature, which could have torn Felix limb from limb with a single blow, did not raise a hand against him. It covered its bleeding face and fled the cottage, stumbling back to its hovel while Felix's curses followed it into the dark.

All night the creature crouched in the hovel, listening. It heard the family's terrified voices through the wall, heard them packing in haste, heard the cart roll away before dawn. When morning came it crept to its chink and looked into an empty cottage. The De Laceys were gone, fled in the night without leaving a trace, and the creature understood that its face alone had been enough to destroy the only happiness it had ever known. It had been kind, it had been gentle, it had asked for nothing but to be tolerated, and its reward was exile.

In the grey morning after the attack, the creature crept back to its hovel like a wounded animal to its den. Its few possessions were there: the straw bed, the books, the memory of a hundred peaceful evenings. It sat among them, holding its bruised head in its hands, and tried to understand what had happened. The old man's kindness had been real; Felix's horror had been real; both were true at once. It was this impossibility that broke the creature's heart more surely than any blow.

Rage came then, black and complete. The creature gathered dry wood and set fire to the cottage, watching the flames devour the little home it had loved and served. It danced around the burning walls, howling its grief to the empty forest, and in that hour it made a vow. If human beings would give it nothing but hatred, it would give them hatred in return. It would find its creator, the man who had made it and abandoned it, and it would demand the justice it had been denied. The hovel, the lessons, the books, the dream of love: all of it went up in smoke with the cottage.

Strangely, the creature could not hate Felix, even then. In its calmer hours it understood that the young man had acted as any devoted son would act, striking down what he believed to be a monster threatening his blind father. It was this understanding that made the rejection so unbearable: there was no villain to blame, no cruelty to condemn, only the brute fact of its own face, which turned love itself into violence. If even a good man's love became a weapon against it, what hope was left anywhere in the world?

In the smoking ruins the creature found a new and terrible clarity. It had tried goodness, and goodness had earned it blows and exile. Very well, then. It would no longer beg for a place among human beings. It would demand one, and the demand would be laid at the feet of the only person who could never refuse to hear it: the man who had made it. Somewhere to the south, in Geneva, Victor Frankenstein was living his comfortable life, and the creature swore that he would not live it in peace much longer.

Before it left the ruined cottage behind, the creature stood in the forest and spoke its vow aloud to the empty trees. It renounced the hope of love and took up the purpose of revenge. It would find Victor Frankenstein, and it would make him feel what it was to be wretched. The words sounded strange and terrible in its own ears, and even as it spoke them the creature felt the last of its gentleness dying. What walked out of that forest toward Geneva was no longer the eager pupil of the De Laceys. It was their avenger.

When it was time to leave, the creature gathered its few treasures: the three books, wrapped carefully against the weather, and the memory of the old man's voice, which it would carry longer than any possession. It took one last look at the blackened hollow where the cottage had stood, and then it turned its back on the only home it had ever known. The forest closed behind it, indifferent as ever, and the creature walked south with the books heavy in its arms and hatred heavier in its heart.

So the creature turned its face toward Geneva, toward Victor Frankenstein. The long journey hardened it. Every village it passed drove it away with stones; every face it saw turned from it in horror. With each rejection the vow burned deeper, until the creature that had once wept over the De Laceys' music became a being with a single purpose. It would confront the man who had given it life, and it would make him answer for what he had done.

The road to Geneva led through the mountains, and even in its bitterness the creature could not remain blind to their majesty. The towering peaks, the roaring torrents, the vast silence of the high Alps spoke to something deep in its solitary soul, and for moments together its hatred ebbed before the sublimity of nature. But the feeling never lasted. Every human dwelling it passed reminded it of doors closed against it, and by the time the lights of Geneva appeared in the valley below, the creature's purpose had hardened into iron.

chapters.title: The Murder of William Frankenstein
paragraphs: On the way to Geneva the creature passed through the woods of Plainpalais, and there it saw a beautiful child playing alone among the trees. The boy was perhaps seven years old, with bright eyes and a fearless laugh, and at the sight of him a desperate hope woke in the creature's heart. Here was a human being too young to have learned prejudice, too innocent to judge by appearances. Perhaps this child would not scream or throw stones. Perhaps this child could be taught to love it. The creature stepped from the trees and approached him.

The creature watched the boy for a long time before it moved, hidden among the trees, studying his carefree movements with a hunger that was almost physical. Here was childhood itself, the innocence it had lost before it ever possessed it. It imagined taking the boy's hand and leading him into the forest, teaching him its own secret language of loneliness, winning from this one unspoiled heart the affection the world denied it. The fantasy gave it courage, and it stepped forward with its arms half-opened, almost smiling.

The hope died within seconds. The boy shrank back in terror at the sight of the towering figure, and when the creature tried to calm him, the child fought and screamed, threatening to tell his father, who would punish the monster. The creature seized him, meaning only to silence his cries, but the boy struggled harder, and then, in his panic, he cried out his name. He was William Frankenstein, Victor's youngest brother. At that word something snapped in the creature's mind. This was no innocent stranger. This was the blood of its creator, the family that had everything while the creature had nothing. Its hands closed around the boy's throat, and did not open again until the small body was still.

The deed itself took only moments, but its meaning unfolded slowly in the creature's mind like poison spreading through the blood. It had killed a child. Whatever justice it claimed against Victor, whatever misery excused its rage, this small still body in the grass was beyond excuse. The creature felt the weight of it settle onto its soul and knew that something in itself had broken that could never be mended. Yet even as it recoiled from what it had done, it clung to the act, for to regret it would be to face the emptiness beneath, and the emptiness was worse than the guilt.

When it was done, the creature stood over the lifeless child in a strange calm. It felt no triumph, only a cold satisfaction, as if a first debt had been paid. It had meant to wound Victor as it had been wounded, and now the wound was dealt. But even as it looked down at William's still face, the creature knew that this was only the beginning. It had crossed a line from which there was no return, and the misery that had made it cruel would now make it crueller still.

Around the boy's neck hung a miniature portrait in a locket, the likeness of a beautiful woman. The creature took it and studied the painted face: Caroline Beaufort Frankenstein, Victor's mother, dead these several years, whose gentle memory the whole family cherished. The creature gazed at the portrait with a bitter fascination. Here was the face of maternal love, the very thing it had never known and would never know. It slipped the locket into its own rough clothing, a trophy of its first revenge.

The creature carried the miniature with it for hours, taking it out again and again to study the serene painted eyes. Alone in the woods it spoke to the portrait, pouring out the story of its wretched existence to the one face that could not turn away. Then, with a sudden fury at its own weakness, it resolved to turn the keepsake into a weapon. The Frankensteins treasured this image; very well, it would become the instrument of their ruin. That night it sought out the sleeping servant girl, and the plan was carried out in silence.

Later that night, wandering near the town, the creature found a young woman sleeping in a barn. It was Justine Moritz, a servant of the Frankenstein household, beloved by them all. The creature looked down at her peaceful face and felt a spasm of hatred, not for her, but for everything she represented: the warmth of a home, the safety of belonging. Silently it slipped the locket with Caroline's portrait into the pocket of Justine's dress. Let them find it there, it thought. Let the Frankensteins learn what it is to lose one they love to injustice, as it had lost everything to injustice.

In the days that followed, the creature lingered near Geneva in secret, watching the grief it had caused unfold. It saw the search parties in the woods, saw the Frankenstein household in mourning, saw suspicion settle like a poison over the innocent Justine. And it felt a dark satisfaction, for this was exactly what it had intended: to make Victor feel, in his own home and among his own loved ones, the same helpless anguish that the creature felt every day of its existence. The war had begun, and the first battle was won.

The creature did not go far after the murder. It hid in the hills above Geneva and watched the town wake to horror: the alarm raised, the search parties combing the woods, the small body carried home through weeping crowds. It watched from its distant perch with a cold, detached curiosity, as if the grief unfolding below belonged to someone else's story. Only when it saw Victor arrive, saw him kneel beside his brother's body, did the creature feel the first stirrings of something like remorse, quickly drowned in satisfaction.

So the creature confessed it afterward, without excuses and without pity for itself. It had murdered the child in a fury of revenge, and it had deliberately laid the guilt at Justine's door. It was the first blow of its war against its creator, and it was struck with a cold deliberation that frightened even the creature itself when it remembered it later. From that night on, Victor Frankenstein would know that his enemy could reach into the very heart of his home.

As it watched Victor's grief, a new resolve formed in the creature's mind. It was not enough for Victor to suffer in ignorance; he had to know whose hand had struck him, and why. The creature decided then that it would confront its creator face to face, tell him the whole history of its wretched life, and demand the one thing that could still save them both. It did not yet know where or when the meeting would happen, only that it must.

From its hiding place the creature studied Victor's face as he mourned, and the sight gave it a dark pleasure. Here at last was the creator suffering as the creature had suffered: helpless, agonised, alone with his guilt. But beneath the pleasure ran a stranger current, a flicker of the pity it had once felt for the De Laceys. For an instant the creature almost wished it could undo what it had done. Then it remembered the stones and the curses, the blows and the flight, and the pity died. The war would go on.

When the creature told this story to Victor on the glacier, it did not flinch or excuse itself. It laid the murder bare in all its horror, as if daring its creator to look at what abandonment had made. Victor listened with a sickness in his soul, for he understood that every detail of the crime led back to his own workshop, to the night he had given life and then fled from it. The blood of William Frankenstein was on the creature's hands, but the guilt, Victor knew, was his own.

chapters.title: The Trial of Justine Moritz
paragraphs: Justine Moritz had been taken into the Frankenstein household as a girl, after her own mother treated her cruelly, and she had grown up to be one of the family's most devoted servants. She was gentle, pious, and loved by everyone, especially by Elizabeth, who treated her more like a sister than a servant. When little William's body was found in the woods, strangled, the whole household was thrown into grief, and Justine wept with the rest of them, never dreaming that suspicion would fall on her.

In prison Justine could not comprehend what had happened to her. She told her story again and again to anyone who would listen: she had spent the night of the murder in a barn outside the town, she had slept deeply, she knew nothing of the locket until it was found in her pocket. Her account never varied, because it was true, but truth without proof is a frail shield. Elizabeth visited her daily, bringing food and comfort, and wept to see her gentle friend wasting away with bewilderment and fear.

The suspicion came from the locket. When Justine was searched, the miniature portrait of Caroline Frankenstein was found hidden in the pocket of her dress, the very locket William had worn around his neck. Justine was bewildered. She had no explanation for how it came to be there, and her confusion looked like guilt. She was arrested and thrown into prison to await trial for murder. The evidence seemed overwhelming: the stolen portrait in her possession, no witness to defend her, no story that could explain it away.

At the trial, the case against her was built on that single piece of evidence, and on the whispers of servants who claimed she had been seen near the woods. Elizabeth Lavenza spoke for her with passionate eloquence, declaring before the court that Justine's character was proof of her innocence, that no one who knew her could believe her capable of such a crime. The judges listened politely, but the locket spoke louder than Elizabeth's tears. The jury found Justine guilty, and she was condemned to die.

Through it all, one man in the courtroom knew the truth, and said nothing. Victor Frankenstein sat through the trial in an agony of guilt, knowing with absolute certainty that the creature he had made was the real murderer. But to speak would have been to confess his own unspeakable secret, to tell the world that he had created a living being and loosed it upon mankind. He feared, too, that no one would believe him, that they would take him for a madman. So he remained silent, and his silence was a second murder, committed in the courtroom itself.

The courtroom was crowded on the day of judgment, for the murder of a child of so respected a family had horrified all of Geneva. The prosecutor displayed the locket before the jury and wove a tale of a servant girl tempted by a valuable trinket and driven to murder for its sake. Witnesses were called who swore they had seen Justine near the woods at dusk. Against all of this, Elizabeth's testimony stood alone, a single voice insisting on the evidence of a blameless life. The judges deliberated only briefly. The law demanded a life for a life, and Justine's was forfeit.

In her cell, Justine was visited by her confessor, who pressed her to confess her guilt and make her peace with God. Terrified of dying unabsolved, the poor girl at last gave way and confessed to a crime she had not committed, hoping that heaven would be more merciful than earth. It was the cruellest twist of all: the innocent condemned herself with her own lips, so that even those who loved her began to doubt.

Once, in the darkest hour of the night before the verdict, Victor came close to speaking. He rose from his bed with the confession on his lips, determined to go to the judges and tell them everything, whatever the cost to himself. But at his chamber door his courage failed. He saw in his mind their incredulous faces, the whispers of madness, the ruin of his father's name, and he turned back. He told himself that the truth would not save Justine now, that no one would believe so wild a tale. It was a coward's reasoning, and he knew it, and it poisoned his sleep for the rest of his life.

On the night before her execution, Elizabeth and Victor visited Justine in her cell, and she wept in Elizabeth's arms, still protesting her innocence even as she prepared to die. The next morning she was led to the scaffold and hanged before a silent crowd. Victor watched from a distance, and her death marked his soul forever. He had created the creature, abandoned it, and now his cowardice had killed an innocent girl as surely as if his own hands had tied the rope.

In the cell, during that last visit, Justine spoke to Elizabeth with a calm that broke her friend's heart. She said she forgave the world that had condemned her, and that she went to her death trusting in a justice higher than man's. She thanked Elizabeth for believing in her when no one else would, and she asked her to remember her kindly. Elizabeth held her hands and wept, and promised through her tears that Justine's name would never be stained in her memory.

Elizabeth never recovered from Justine's death. She who had defended her friend so passionately now reproached herself for not having done more, for not having found the words that would have saved her. She confessed to Victor that her faith in human justice was broken, that she no longer knew how to believe in a world where the innocent could die so. Victor read her words with a heart like lead, for he alone knew how right she was, and how useless his knowledge had been.

After the execution Victor fell into a fever of remorse that nearly killed him. He wandered the streets of Geneva like a ghost, starting at every sound, seeing Justine's face in his dreams, hearing her voice accusing him from the scaffold. He knew that he could have saved her with a single word, and that his fear had killed her. It was this guilt, as much as grief for William, that drove him at last to flee Geneva for the mountains above Chamonix, where, on the ice, his enemy was waiting to confront him.

The household fell into a heavy mourning. Victor's father, already aged by grief, seemed to shrink before their eyes, and the servants moved through the house in silence. Little was said, but much was felt: the sense of a curse hanging over the family, of happiness withdrawn. Even Ernest, Victor's younger brother, who had always been cheerful, grew quiet and withdrawn. The Frankenstein home, once the happiest in Geneva, became a house of shadows, and Victor, knowing himself the author of it all, could barely endure to remain under its roof.

All Geneva talked of nothing but the trial for weeks afterward. The town that had admired the Frankensteins now whispered about them: a murdered child, a hanged servant, a family under a shadow no one could name. Some said Justine must have been guilty after all; others, who had known her, shook their heads and spoke of a justice that had failed. Through it all Victor moved like a man already condemned, carrying a secret heavier than any sentence the court could have passed.

chapters.title: Elizabeth Lavenza
paragraphs: Elizabeth Lavenza had been part of Victor's life for as long as he could remember. She was the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman who had died in poverty, and Victor's parents had taken her into their home when she was a small child. She grew up alongside Victor as his cherished companion, beautiful, kind, and accomplished, and as they grew older their childish affection ripened into a deep and promised love. When Victor's mother Caroline lay dying, she joined their hands together and made them promise that they would one day marry, and they gave the promise with all their hearts.

After Caroline's death it was Elizabeth who held the household together. She comforted the grieving father, she mothered little William, she governed the servants with a gentle authority beyond her years. Justine adored her, and it was said in Geneva that where Elizabeth was, there was peace. Victor, watching from the distance of his studies and then of his secret labour, loved her all the more for the steadiness she brought to a house shadowed by loss. She was, in every true sense, the heart of the Frankenstein family.

During Victor's years at the university of Ingolstadt, it was Elizabeth's letters that kept him tied to the world he had left behind. She wrote of life in Geneva, of his father's health, of little William's games, and of her own quiet days, filling her pages with a gentle warmth that reproached him, without ever reproaching, for his long silence. She begged him to come home, sensing, with a woman's intuition, that some secret trouble weighed on him. Victor read her letters with a breaking heart, for he could never tell her what that trouble was.

After the deaths of William and Justine, and after Victor's long illness and his terrible journey through the mountains, the family urged him to keep the promise he had made at his mother's deathbed. Elizabeth, who had waited for him faithfully through all the years of his absence and his strangeness, asked only for his happiness. Victor agreed to the marriage, though a shadow lay over his consent. He believed, with a fatal misunderstanding, that the creature's threat to be with him on his wedding night meant that the monster intended to kill him, and he resolved that he would meet his enemy at last, even if it cost him his life.

In the weeks before the wedding, Elizabeth watched her bridegroom with growing unease. Victor was distracted and feverish, starting at sudden noises, wandering the house at night with a pistol he tried to hide from her. When she asked him gently what troubled him, he could only embrace her and beg her not to question him, promising that after their wedding night all would be explained. Elizabeth, who trusted him utterly, accepted his silence, but her letters to her friends in those days were full of a nameless dread she could not name.

The wedding day dawned fair, and for a few hours it seemed that happiness might return. The ceremony was small and quiet, attended by the family's closest friends. Elizabeth was radiant in her bridal dress, and when she took Victor's hand her smile held all the trust in the world. Victor tried to match her joy, but those who looked closely saw the strain in his face, the way his eyes kept straying to the windows and the doors. He was a bridegroom already listening for an enemy's step.

The wedding took place quietly, and for a few hours Victor allowed himself to hope. Elizabeth was radiant, and her joy seemed to push back the darkness that had surrounded him for so long. They travelled to Evian, to a quiet inn on the lake, for their wedding night. But Victor could not rest. As evening fell he grew restless and fearful, and when Elizabeth retired to their room, he took a pistol and a dagger and began to patrol the corridors of the inn, listening for the slightest sound, convinced that the creature would come for him in the dark.

On the wedding night, after Elizabeth retired to the bridal chamber, she lay awake listening to her husband's footsteps pacing the corridor outside. She had expected joy and tenderness; instead there was this strange vigil, this armed watch against some unseen danger. She told herself it was nerves, the aftermath of all they had suffered. She did not know that Victor was guarding the wrong door, and that death was already climbing toward her window.

It was the last and most terrible of his mistakes. While Victor guarded the stairs with his weapons ready, the creature slipped silently through the window of the bridal chamber. Elizabeth's scream tore through the inn, a sound Victor would hear in his dreams for the rest of his life. He rushed to the room and found her lifeless upon the bed, her beautiful face marked by the violence of the hands that had taken her life. The threat had never been aimed at him. It had been aimed at everything he loved, and it had found its mark.

They say that in her last moments Elizabeth understood nothing of what was happening, only that some terrible shadow had fallen across her happiness. She had gone to her bridal chamber full of joy, thinking of the life she and Victor would share, of the children they would raise, of the peace they would know at last. The creature that came through the window brought none of the explanations Victor had promised. It brought only the swift, merciless violence with which it had learned to answer the world.

Victor's reason nearly left him then, and his father's heart broke under the final blow. The old man, who had already buried his wife and his youngest son, could not survive the loss of Elizabeth, and he died within days. Victor was left utterly alone, with no family to protect and nothing to live for but revenge. He buried his dead, bought pistols and daggers, and set out after the creature with the fury of a man who has nothing more to lose.

After the funerals, Victor went alone to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth, and his father lay buried side by side. Kneeling on the cold earth, he raised his hands to the heavens and swore a solemn oath: he would hunt the creature to the ends of the earth and destroy it, or die in the attempt. He called on the spirits of the dead to witness his vow. It was a terrible oath, and it gave his shattered life a single terrible purpose. From that hour Victor Frankenstein lived for one thing only: revenge.

Long afterward, when the creature stood weeping over Victor's lifeless body in Walton's cabin, it spoke of Elizabeth among its other victims, and its voice broke with a remorse deeper than any it had shown before. Of all its crimes, it said, the murder of Elizabeth was the one that haunted it most, for she had been innocent even of knowing its name. The creature had meant to wound Victor, but in killing Elizabeth it felt it had murdered the best of mankind, and the knowledge was a torment no revenge could sweeten.

In Victor's memory Elizabeth remained forever as she had been in life: gentle, patient, and good, the one person whose love had never wavered. Her death completed the creature's design with a terrible symmetry. The creature had been left utterly alone by its creator's abandonment, and now, by murdering everyone Victor loved, it had made Victor as alone as itself. Creator and creature, bound together by grief and hatred, had nothing left now but each other, and the frozen waste of the Arctic waiting to receive them both.
